text:
**Short answer:** For a typical full-size fridge, look for a station with a **surge rating of at least 1,300 W** and **about 1,500–2,000 Wh** of battery if you want roughly a day of backup. Smaller stations can work for shorter outages.

**The three things to check**

1. **Surge (startup) watts.** The compressor draws a brief spike when it starts. [HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/) uses 1,200 W as its startup figure. [powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator) uses 1,300 W, and notes that the real number depends on your fridge. [BlackBoxSupplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage) gives 1,200–2,400 W for household fridges, with larger or older units at the high end. If the surge rating is too low, the station shuts off when the fridge tries to start, no matter how much battery it has.

2. **Continuous watts.** Most full-size fridges run at about 100–250 W while the compressor is on. Almost any station rated for 1,000 W or more handles that easily. [BlackBoxSupplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage) also recommends a pure sine wave inverter.

3. **Watt-hours (energy).** The compressor runs only about a third of the time, so the average draw is much lower than the label's running watts. For example, an ENERGY STAR 18 cu ft fridge averages about 41 W, or about 991 Wh per day. Adding inverter losses and a safety margin brings that to about 1,400 Wh per day ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)). To estimate your own fridge, find its annual kWh on the yellow EnergyGuide label, then calculate: kWh/year × 1,000 ÷ 8,760 = average watts.

**Roughly how long different sizes last**

Using HomeGridHQ's assumptions (150 W running, 1,200 W startup, 35% duty cycle, 85% efficiency), [HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/) lists these runtimes:
- ~1,000 Wh (e.g., Jackery Explorer 1000 v2, 1,070 Wh): about 17 hours
- ~2,000 Wh (e.g., Jackery Explorer 2000 v2, 2,042 Wh): about 33 hours

Actual runtime depends on how warm the room is and how often the door opens. [BlackBoxSupplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage) suggests about 1,000 Wh for most of a day and 1,600–2,000 Wh for a full 24 hours.

**Tips**
- Keep the fridge door shut during the outage. [HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/) cites USDA guidance that food is unsafe after 4 hours above 40°F with the door closed.
- Check the station's listed surge rating, not just its battery size.
- Rated capacity is higher than usable AC energy, so leave some margin.

**Example product:** The [BLUETTI AC200L](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac200l) (2,048 Wh, 2,400 W continuous, 3,600 W surge-rated "Power Lifting") fits these requirements.
